title: Stability
statement:
Weakly étale morphisms, as defined in [sk-def-pe-morphisms] and [def-weil-weakly-etale-morphism], are stable under base change and
composition, and the property is local on source and target for the Zariski topology.
Every $X$-morphism between two weakly étale $X$-schemes is weakly étale. Affine pro-étale
morphisms (affine spectra of ind-étale ring maps [def-weil-pbc-ind-etale-algebra]) are stable under affine base change and composition.

proof.text: Let $f:U\to X$ be weakly étale and $X^{\prime}\to X$ arbitrary. Put $U^{\prime}=U\times_X X^{\prime}$. Both $f$ and $\Delta_f$ are flat by definition. The universal property of fibre products identifies $U^{\prime}\times_{X^{\prime}}U^{\prime}$ with $(U\times_XU)\times_XX^{\prime}$, and identifies $\Delta_{f^{\prime}}$ with the base change of $\Delta_f$ along its projection to $U\times_XU$. Thus base-change stability of flatness applies to both $f^{\prime}$ and its diagonal, proving that $f^{\prime}$ is weakly étale.

Let $V\xrightarrow{g}U\xrightarrow{f}X$ be weakly étale. Flatness of $g$ and $f$ gives flatness of $f\circ g$. Its diagonal factors as $V\xrightarrow{\Delta_g}V\times_UV\xrightarrow{j}V\times_XV$. The defining equalities for these fibre products give $V\times_UV\simeq(V\times_XV)\times_{U\times_XU}U$, where the maps to $U\times_XU$ are $g\times_Xg$ and $\Delta_f$. Consequently $j$ is a base change of the flat map $\Delta_f$, while $\Delta_g$ is flat by hypothesis. Their composite is flat by transitivity. This proves weak étaleness of $f\circ g$.

Flatness is local on source and target directly from its stalkwise definition: restricting either scheme to an open neighbourhood changes neither local ring nor its induced homomorphism. For open subschemes $U_0\subset U$, $X_0\subset X$ with $f(U_0)\subset X_0$, the fibre product $U_0\times_{X_0}U_0$ identifies with the open subscheme $p_1^{-1}(U_0)\cap p_2^{-1}(U_0)$ of $U\times_XU$. Indeed both descriptions represent pairs of maps into $U_0$ agreeing over $X$; they agree over $X_0$ because an open immersion is an inclusion of an open subscheme. Under this identification the restricted diagonal is $\Delta_f|_{U_0}$. Therefore restrictions of a weakly étale morphism are weakly étale. Conversely, if $X=\bigcup_aX_a$ and $f^{-1}(X_a)=\bigcup_bU_{ab}$ with all $U_{ab}\to X_a$ weakly étale, each $u\in U$ belongs to one $U_{ab}$, so the local homomorphisms for $f$ at $u$ and for $\Delta_f$ at $u$ are those for the restricted maps and are flat. Thus $f$ and $\Delta_f$ are flat everywhere. This proves both Zariski locality assertions without any separatedness assumption.

proof.text: Let $a:U\to X$, $b:V\to X$ be weakly étale and let $h:U\to V$ satisfy $b\circ h=a$. Factor $h$ through its graph $\gamma_h:U\to U\times_XV$ and the second projection $p_2$. The graph is the base change of $\Delta_b:V\to V\times_XV$ along $(h\circ p_1,p_2):U\times_XV\to V\times_XV$: the pullback condition forces the second component to equal $h$ of the first. Hence $\gamma_h$ is flat. The projection $p_2$ is a base change of $a$, hence flat, so $h$ is flat. For the diagonal, the square with top $\Delta_h:U\to U\times_VU$, bottom $\Delta_a:U\to U\times_XU$, left identity and right the canonical map is cartesian. To verify this, maps from any test scheme into its pullback are a pair $(u_1,u_2)$ with $h u_1=h u_2$, together with $u$ with $(u_1,u_2)=(u,u)$; the extra equality follows from $h u=h u$, so the datum is exactly $u$. Thus $\Delta_h$ is a base change of the flat $\Delta_a$ and is flat. By definition $h$ is weakly étale.

proof.text: For $R\to B$ ind-étale and any $R\to R^{\prime}$, the affine fibre-product theorem identifies the base change of $\operatorname{Spec}B\to\operatorname{Spec}R$ with $\operatorname{Spec}(B\otimes_RR^{\prime})\to\operatorname{Spec}R^{\prime}$, with structure map $r^{\prime}\mapsto1\otimes r^{\prime}$. The base-change clause of ind-étale stability says this ring map is ind-étale. Hence its spectrum is affine pro-étale in the stated sense. For $R\to B\to C$ with both maps ind-étale, the composition clause says $R\to C$ is ind-étale; its spectrum is precisely the composite of the given affine pro-étale maps. These are the two final assertions. The definitions here are the ind-étale/affine-spectrum definitions of sk-def-pe-morphisms, not the assertion that every weakly étale morphism admits a global ind-étale presentation.
